newsitem.title: FRANCE: Wartime expropriations in Paris under scrutiny.
newsitem.headline: Wartime expropriations in Paris under scrutiny.

text.p: The French Left wants an official inquiry to determine whether some of the apartments acquired by the Paris city council during World War Two were seized from Jews deported to Nazi death camps.

The daily newspaper Le Monde said on Saturday the Socialists would request on Monday that a committee which includes members of the Jewish community investigate the history of the property in question.

Historians' long-standing suspicions that some of the city property was seized from Jews was revived by a book published recently that coincides with the Paris city council selling off part of its real estate following a political scandal.
"Private Estate" by journalist Brigitte Vital-Durand looks into an area of the capital's mediaeval Marais central district where part of the Jewish community still lives.
She said the area's population had dropped from 25,000 to 5,000 during the war as Jewish families were deported or fled and hundreds of buildings were destroyed for urban renovation.

Vital-Durand said the Paris city council now owns 150 buildings in the area, some of which had belonged to Jews who never returned after the war. She had no global figure for the number of Paris dwellings that may have been seized from Jews.

The issue has acquired fresh urgency as Paris mayor Jean Tiberi has ordered the sale of a third of the 1,389 apartments the city has purchased or acquired over the centuries through donations and expropriations.
Deputy mayor Jean-Francois Legaret said none of the blocks sold so far or up for sale had belonged to Jewish families.

But Vital-Durand said some property was sold without its history being disclosed, and Communist city councillor Henri Malberg called for the sale to be halted while the origin of the estate is being investigated.
The sale followed a scandal over disclosures that the city council was leasing flats well below market prices to political cronies and notables, including Prime Minister Alain Juppe and relatives.
The scandal forced Juppe to move from his elegant, low-rent Left Bank flat, and has put Tiberi and President Jacques Chirac, the former Paris mayor, under fire.
